key_points: arrays use contiguous memory, linked lists use nodes with pointers
arrays give O(1) random access by index
linked lists allow O(1) insertion and deletion at a known position
arrays have better cache locality
questions.model_answer: Arrays store elements contiguously, giving O(1) indexed access but O(n) inserts in the middle. Linked lists chain nodes with pointers, so inserts/deletes at a known node are O(1) but access is O(n). Choose arrays for frequent random access, linked lists for frequent insertions and deletions.
questions.question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list. When would you choose one over the other?

key_points: a hash function maps keys to bucket indices
collisions are resolved with chaining or open addressing
the load factor triggers resizing/rehashing
average O(1) lookups, worst case O(n)
questions.model_answer: A hash map hashes each key to a bucket index, giving average O(1) get/put. Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing, and the table resizes when the load factor gets too high. Worst case degrades to O(n) with many collisions.
questions.question: What is a hash map and how does it achieve average O(1) lookups?

key_points: two indices move through the data structure toward or along each other
typically applied to sorted arrays
example: pair-sum or removing duplicates
reduces a brute-force O(n^2) solution to O(n)
questions.model_answer: Two pointers walk an array from both ends (or at different speeds), exploiting sorted order to find pairs or windows in one pass. Classic example: finding two numbers that sum to a target in a sorted array in O(n) time instead of O(n^2).
questions.question: Describe the two-pointer technique and give an example problem it solves efficiently.

key_points: divide and conquer: partition around a pivot
average case O(n log n)
worst case O(n^2) with bad pivot choices
in-place with O(log n) recursion stack
questions.model_answer: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then recurses. Average time is O(n log n); worst case is O(n^2) when pivots are consistently bad, e.g. an already-sorted array with a naive pivot.
questions.question: How does quicksort work? What are its average and worst-case time complexities?

key_points: stack is LIFO, queue is FIFO
stack use case: undo history, call stack, depth-first search
queue use case: task scheduling, breadth-first search
both can be built on arrays or linked lists
questions.model_answer: A stack is last-in-first-out (push/pop) and suits undo history or the call stack; a queue is first-in-first-out (enqueue/dequeue) and suits job scheduling or BFS. Both are easily implemented over arrays or linked lists.
questions.question: Explain how a stack and a queue differ, and name a real use case for each.

key_points: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow and fast pointers
the fast pointer moves twice as fast as the slow one
if they meet, a cycle exists
O(n) time and O(1) extra space
questions.model_answer: Use Floyd's cycle detection: advance one pointer one step and another two steps. If the fast pointer meets the slow one, there is a cycle. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
questions.question: How would you detect a cycle in a linked list? Explain the time and space complexity of your approach.

key_points: encapsulation: hide internal state behind methods
inheritance: subclasses reuse and extend base classes
polymorphism: same interface, different behavior
abstraction: expose only essential details
questions.model_answer: The four pillars are encapsulation (bundling data with methods and hiding internals), inheritance (deriving classes from base classes), polymorphism (one interface, many implementations), and abstraction (hiding complexity behind simple interfaces).
questions.question: Name and briefly explain the four pillars of object-oriented programming.

key_points: ArrayList is backed by a resizable array
LinkedList is a doubly-linked list of nodes
ArrayList gives O(1) random access, LinkedList O(n)
LinkedList inserts/deletes in O(1) at a known node; ArrayList shifts elements
questions.model_answer: ArrayList wraps a resizable array: O(1) indexed access but O(n) mid-list inserts. LinkedList chains nodes: O(1) insert/delete at a known position but O(n) traversal. Prefer ArrayList for read-heavy workloads.
questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList in Java?

key_points: declarative, lazy pipeline for processing data
intermediate operations vs terminal operations
streams do not mutate the source collection
can run in parallel with parallelStream
questions.model_answer: Streams express data processing as lazy pipelines of intermediate operations (map, filter) ending in a terminal operation (collect, forEach). Unlike collections they don't store data or mutate the source, and they can easily parallelize.
questions.question: What are Java Streams and how do they differ from collections?

key_points: checked exceptions must be declared or caught, e.g. IOException
unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException, e.g. NullPointerException
use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions
use unchecked exceptions for programming errors
questions.model_answer: Checked exceptions (IOException) are enforced at compile time and suit recoverable failures the caller should handle. Unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses) signal programming bugs and don't require declaration.
questions.question: Explain checked versus unchecked exceptions in Java, and when you would use each.

key_points: automatic reclamation of unreachable objects
young generation: eden plus survivor spaces
old (tenured) generation for long-lived objects
minor GC is frequent and cheap; major GC is rarer and costlier
questions.model_answer: The GC frees objects no longer reachable from GC roots. The heap is split into a young generation (eden + survivors, collected by cheap minor GCs) and an old generation for survivors that age out, collected by costlier major GCs.
questions.question: What happens during garbage collection in the JVM? What are the heap generations?

key_points: acquires the intrinsic (monitor) lock of an object
guarantees mutual exclusion for the critical section
can cause deadlock when locks are acquired in inconsistent order
alternatives: java.util.concurrent locks, atomic classes, immutable data
questions.model_answer: synchronized acquires an object's intrinsic lock so only one thread executes the block at a time. Misuse causes deadlocks (locks taken in different orders), contention, and poor scalability; prefer java.util.concurrent utilities where possible.
questions.question: How does the synchronized keyword work in Java, and what problems can it cause?

key_points: inversion of control: dependencies are provided, not created
the Spring IoC container manages bean lifecycles
injection via constructor, setter, or field (@Autowired)
constructor injection is the preferred style
questions.model_answer: Dependency injection hands object creation to the Spring IoC container, which wires beans together at startup. Constructor injection with @Autowired (implicit on a single constructor) is preferred because it makes dependencies explicit and testable.
questions.question: What is dependency injection, and how does Spring Boot implement it?

key_points: meta-annotation combining three annotations
@Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, @ComponentScan
auto-configuration sets up beans based on the classpath
component scanning starts from the annotated class's package
questions.model_answer: @SpringBootApplication combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. It triggers auto-configuration from classpath dependencies and scans the package subtree for components, and it marks the class containing the main() entry point.
questions.question: What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation do?

key_points: @RestController marks the class as a REST handler
@RequestMapping / @GetMapping / @PostMapping map URLs
@PathVariable and @RequestBody bind request data
return values are serialized to JSON by Jackson
questions.model_answer: Annotate a class with @RestController, map methods with @GetMapping/@PostMapping under a @RequestMapping path, bind inputs with @PathVariable/@RequestBody, and Spring serializes the returned objects to JSON via Jackson.
questions.question: How do you build a REST endpoint in Spring Boot? Mention the key annotations.

key_points: extend JpaRepository to get CRUD methods for free
method names are parsed into queries
example: findByLastNameOrderByFirstNameAsc
@Query allows custom JPQL or native SQL
questions.model_answer: Extending JpaRepository gives you save/find/delete out of the box. Derived query methods like findByEmail are parsed from their names into JPQL, and @Query covers anything the naming convention can't express.
questions.question: Explain Spring Data JPA repositories. How do derived query methods work?

key_points: requests pass through a servlet filter chain
authentication happens before authorization
stateless APIs commonly use JWT bearer tokens
rules are configured in a SecurityFilterChain bean
questions.model_answer: Spring Security inserts filters into the servlet chain: authentication filters validate credentials (often JWT bearer tokens for stateless APIs), then authorization filters enforce access rules declared in a SecurityFilterChain bean.
questions.question: How does Spring Security protect a REST API? Describe the filter chain at a high level.

key_points: props are passed from the parent and are read-only
state is internal to the component and mutable via its setter
state updates trigger a re-render
lift state up to share it between components
questions.model_answer: Props flow down from parents and must not be mutated; state is owned by the component and updated through its setter, which schedules a re-render. Shared state lives in the closest common ancestor.
questions.question: What is the difference between props and state in React?

key_points: useState declares reactive component state
useEffect runs side effects after render
the dependency array controls when the effect re-runs
effects can return a cleanup function
questions.model_answer: useState gives you a state value plus a setter that re-renders on change. useEffect runs side effects like fetching after render; its dependency array decides when it re-runs, and returning a function provides cleanup on unmount or re-run.
questions.question: Explain the useState and useEffect hooks with a simple example of each.

key_points: the virtual DOM is an in-memory representation of the UI
React diffs the new tree against the previous one
only the changed real DOM nodes are updated
stable keys help React match list items during diffing
questions.model_answer: The virtual DOM is a lightweight tree React keeps in memory. On each render React diffs it against the previous tree (reconciliation) and patches only the real DOM nodes that changed; stable keys make list diffing accurate and fast.
questions.question: What is the virtual DOM, and how does reconciliation work?

key_points: fetch inside useEffect so it runs after render
track loading and error in state
cancel in-flight requests with AbortController on cleanup
guard against race conditions from overlapping requests
questions.model_answer: Call fetch inside useEffect, keep loading/error/data in state, and abort the request in the effect cleanup with AbortController to avoid setting state on unmounted components or stale responses winning a race.
questions.question: How do you fetch data in a React component? Cover loading and error states.

key_points: they prevent wasted re-renders and recomputation
useMemo caches an expensive computed value
useCallback caches a function reference for memoized children
React.memo skips re-rendering when props are unchanged; profile before adding
questions.model_answer: These memoization tools skip work when inputs haven't changed: useMemo caches expensive values, useCallback keeps stable function identities for memoized children, and React.memo bails out of re-renders with equal props. Only add them where profiling shows a real cost.
questions.question: When would you use useMemo, useCallback, or React.memo? What problem do they solve?

key_points: concise professional summary, not your life story
highlight skills relevant to the role
connect your background to this position
keep it under two minutes
questions.model_answer: Give a 60-90 second arc: who you are professionally, 2-3 relevant strengths with brief proof, and why this role is the natural next step. End by tying your goals to the team's mission.
questions.question: Tell me about yourself.

key_points: show you researched the company specifically
connect their mission or values to yours
tie the role to your skills and growth
sound genuine, not flattering
questions.model_answer: Reference something specific — a product, engineering blog post, or value — explain why it resonates with you, and connect the role's responsibilities to what you do well and want to grow into.
questions.question: Why do you want to work at this company?

key_points: use the STAR structure: situation, task, action, result
reproduced the bug before attempting a fix
describe your debugging process and tools
share what you learned or changed afterwards
questions.model_answer: Walk through STAR: set the scene, explain how you reproduced and isolated the issue (logs, debugger, bisecting), describe the fix and verification, and close with the lesson or process improvement it led to.
questions.question: Describe a challenging bug you fixed. How did you approach it?

key_points: describe a specific, real disagreement
show you listened to the other perspective
focus on the shared goal, not winning
end with the outcome and what it taught you
questions.model_answer: Pick a genuine technical disagreement, show you sought to understand their reasoning first, explain how you compared options against team goals (sometimes with a prototype or data), and share the resolution and takeaway.
questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate. How did you handle it?

key_points: name a real, work-relevant weakness
show concrete steps you take to manage it
avoid disguised strengths or clichés
demonstrate self-awareness and growth
questions.model_answer: Name an honest weakness (e.g. over-committing, discomfort delegating), give a brief example, then spend most of the answer on the specific habits or systems you now use to counteract it and the progress you've seen.
questions.question: What is your greatest weakness?

key_points: state the project's goal and scope clearly
isolate exactly what you personally did
explain a technical decision you made and why
quantify the outcome where possible
questions.model_answer: Frame the project and its goal, zoom in on your specific contributions and one meaningful technical decision (with trade-offs), then quantify the result — users served, latency cut, bugs reduced — and what you'd do differently.
questions.question: Describe a project you are proud of and your specific contribution to it.
